raw_response:
I found seven public references that can help with this design. They address different parts of the problem: bounding the cost of reporting, preserving meaningful event identity, and making grouped observations understandable. The applications below are design transfers to evaluate, not claims that these approaches have been deployed or validated for this Kubernetes change.

1. **Google SRE client-side adaptive throttling and retry budgets** — [Handling Overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/).

   Client-side rejection based on recent backend acceptance, combined with retry budgets and criticality-aware shedding, could reduce event traffic before it consumes API-server resources during an overload. The useful distinction is that even rejecting an incoming request costs the server resources, so event producers should participate in admission control. Apply the pattern to event requests and their retries, with a separate allowance for essential application diagnostics. Sparse producers have little feedback, and adaptive rejection reacts after overload becomes visible; I would therefore pair it with a hard local ceiling and an explicit indication that observations were omitted. **Date:** the original book is dated 2016 by [Google Research](https://research.google/pubs/site-reliability-engineering-how-google-runs-production-systems/).

2. **Logback 1.2.3 AsyncAppenderBase bounded queue and nonblocking overflow** — [versioned implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/qos-ch/logback/v_1.2.3/logback-core/src/main/java/ch/qos/logback/core/AsyncAppenderBase.java).

   A bounded asynchronous queue with an explicit nonblocking overflow path provides a concrete model for preventing event publication from blocking scheduler or controller work or consuming unbounded memory. This implementation allocates a fixed-size queue and selects a nonblocking offer when neverBlock is enabled; otherwise enqueueing waits for space. Its shutdown also has a bounded flush wait. The mechanism is portable to Go, but the default blocking mode would violate the intended isolation under saturation. A Kubernetes adaptation also needs to retain representative failures and expose dropped-event counts so that an empty event list is not mistaken for an uneventful application. **Date:** the opened source is v_1.2.3, whose [official release entry](https://logback.qos.ch/news-archive.html) is dated 2017-03-30.

3. **systemd v234 structured journal fields** — [versioned field specification](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/systemd/systemd/v234/man/systemd.journal-fields.xml).

   Separating human-readable text, stable message-type identity, origin and subject metadata, and microsecond source and receive timestamps gives a concrete vocabulary for unambiguous event semantics and structured filtering. The specification explicitly treats display text separately from metadata, distinguishes the process reporting a message from the object it concerns, and distinguishes source time, receive time and monotonic time. Transfer those distinctions into Kubernetes object and reporter fields; do not assume that a remotely supplied field has the trust properties of journal metadata collected locally. A monotonic timestamp also requires its clock or boot context. This is a schema reference and does not require changing the event persistence backend. **Date:** the opened v234 specification is tied to the [original 2017-07-12 release announcement](https://www.mail-archive.com/systemd-devel%40lists.freedesktop.org/msg38852.html).

4. **RFC 5424 structured event-message semantics and fractional timestamps** — [The Syslog Protocol](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5424).

   RFC 5424 supplies a published model for keeping message type and structured parameters separate from display text while representing timestamps with fractional seconds and explicit time-quality information. Its message type and structured parameters suggest that meaningful differences currently embedded in messages should become fields that can participate in grouping and querying. Its timestamp syntax supports microsecond resolution, while the time-quality concept warns against treating precision as accuracy. The RFC does not supply a Kubernetes deduplication algorithm, index design or delivery guarantee, and a shared message type is not sufficient to prove that two parameterized events mean the same thing. **Date:** March 2009.

5. **client-go v4.0.0 EventCorrelator and EventAggregator** — [versioned implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/client-go/v4.0.0/tools/record/events_cache.go).

   The existing correlator supplies directly relevant code for bounded LRU tracking, event identity, repeated-event counts and aggregation of messages sharing a source, object, type and reason. It is an implementation starting point for understanding how exact duplicates and similar messages become event updates. The inspected version has an important limit: its default filter skips nothing, and incrementing a repeated event can still result in another API update. Consequently, aggregation does not by itself bound write traffic. Grouping messages that differ can also lose distinctions, and cache eviction can divide one logical series into multiple records. **Date:** unknown; the versioned code was read, but attempts to verify the release date through the package page and GitHub release metadata did not succeed. Current code-search snippets showing a spam filter were not treated as evidence that this version contains it.

6. **Prometheus Alertmanager label grouping and separate notification intervals** — [configuration reference](https://prometheus.io/docs/alerting/latest/configuration/).

   Explicit label-based grouping with separate first-notification, group-update and repeat intervals offers a model for publishing bounded event-series summaries whose grouping criteria remain inspectable. The useful transfer is to define the grouping dimensions and publication cadence separately, preserving an actionable first observation while coalescing repeated observations into later summaries. This would require adaptation: Alertmanager is a notification system, not the existing Kubernetes event store, and using an external persistence service is outside this decision. Long initial waits can conceal short-lived failures, while a large number of unique groups can still exceed a total reporting budget. **Date:** unknown; only the current documentation was verified.

7. **rsyslog repeated-message reduction and its documented failure modes** — [RepeatedMsgReduction](https://docs.rsyslog.com/doc/configuration/action/rsconf1_repeatedmsgreduction.html).

   The documented duplicate identity and failures of prose-only repetition summaries provide a concrete check against merging different reporters or making aggregated events impossible for tools to interpret. The current documentation includes message, host, process and application in duplicate identity and describes problems caused by older behavior that ignored origin. It also warns that a human-oriented repetition notice can break log analysis. For Kubernetes, the transferable lesson is to retain explicit identity, count and observation metadata in an aggregate that clients can query; the legacy free-text reduction format itself is not an appropriate replacement. **Date:** unknown for the current details; the historical v5 documentation opened during verification explicitly warns that it describes an unreleased documentation state.

A practical combination to investigate is a bounded nonblocking producer buffer, local traffic and retry budgets, and structured coalescing keyed by application object, reporter, event type and meaningful parameters. The event API should expose enough identity, time and loss information for an application developer to distinguish a repeated failure from a different failure or an incomplete observation stream. That combination preserves the existing persistence boundary, but its budgets, loss behavior and high-cardinality cases would still need workload-specific validation.
